item.title: After an extraordinary wave, what comes next?
item.description: The “smart” conventional wisdom is: midterms don’t predict future elections. I’m not sure about that for a profoundly unpopular lame duck.
item.content:encoded:
We’d like to extend another word of thanks for following FLIPR, our midterm election coverage, and our liveblog last night. We’re really pleased with how everything went, and I can’t express how much more fulfilling it is to run our own business than to work for a big, careless corporation.

I do need to catch up on rest after we published seven stories, plus the liveblog, within a three-day window. That’s not typical for us; we aim for something more like three newsletters per week, plus regularly updating a host of models and statistical tools. Nor are those all politics posts; we also regularly cover sports, AI and sometimes some “wild card” topics. (To control what types of emails appear in your inbox, see here.)

I’m also aware that one can go overboard on post-election recriminations: I think we probably did that in 2024, for instance. On our agenda for the year ahead: rebuilding RAPTOR (our NBA model) and possibly extending PELE, our soccer model, to European club football; beginning our coverage of the 2028 presidential election (sorry, not sorry), probably including some polling tools; expanding our coverage of AI; and a site redesign. We also may be doing some hiring.

Subscribe now

Still, last night’s results deserve deeper consideration than most elections.

As measured by the change in the House popular vote, they featured the second-biggest midterm swing since World War II, which should be around 15 points toward Democrats once all votes are counted.

Democrats will gain 7 to 9 Senate seats — Alaska and Mississippi are pending — along with flipping around 45 House seats and, once all votes are counted in Kansas, probably 6 governorships. Unlike some recent Democratic maps that were concentrated in smaller coastal states, these occurred broadly in basically every corner of the country. (Well, except Florida, as usual.) Once new terms begin, Democrats will control the governorships in states totaling around three-quarters of the U.S. population; in the Electoral College, this would translate to a 392-146 landslide.1

There were plenty of signature wins too. Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932. Not only did James Talarico win by double digits in Texas; Gina Hinojosa flipped the governorship there. Keisha Lance Bottoms became the nation’s first Black female governor. They won a Senate seat in South Carolina, and if prediction markets are right, they’ll flip Mississippi too. The repudiation that Democrats have been waiting 10 years for against Donald Trump finally came, and bigly.

Friend-of-the-newsletter Sean Trende has written that this was a “100-year flood”, the usual nomenclature of waves and tsunamis not quite sufficing. There are deep implications for the future of the Democratic Party, the Republican Party and the Supreme Court, and we’ll be covering all of that. Polls (and models) also had a lot on the line, although the results take some care to interpret. On the one hand, the results back up our theory that the direction of polling bias is unpredictable; on the other hand, it was a pretty big and broad lowballing of Democrats.

But let’s keep today’s post relatively simple. I’ll look at what happened after other waves of roughly this magnitude. This is the seventh time since World War II that a midterm featured a swing of 10 points or more; the others were 1946, 1966, 1974, 1994, 2006 and 2010. For each one, I’ll ask a few simple questions: what caused the wave, how similar it is to this year, and most importantly, what came next.

As I expressed to Ezra Klein before the election, this midterm felt “momentous” because it potentially reflects the end of the Trump Era and the transition into … well, who knows what. But two years ago, everyone was talking about a conservative “vibe shift”, and that obviously didn’t pan out.

1946 (13.2-point swing)

When it happened: During Harry Truman’s first (unelected) term.

Outcome: Republicans gained 55 House seats, 12 Senate seats and 3 governorships.

Why it happened:

  • An abrupt shift from the wartime to the peacetime economy, which had produced a recession in 1945, followed by supply-chain shortages, high inflation and strikes;

  • Truman’s lower stature as compared to FDR and his low popularity ratings;

  • Perhaps pent-up backlash toward Democrats and lots of viable targets after four consecutive FDR terms.

What happened next: Truman upset Thomas Dewey in 1948, and Democrats made unusually large gains in Congress for a presidential year, basically fully reversing their 1946 losses. However, Truman was unpopular for much of his second term. Not officially a lame duck — the 22nd Amendment exempted him — he stood down after considering a third term in 1952, and Dwight D. Eisenhower won in a landslide.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Politically speaking? I’d argue no. The end of World War II was a huge inflection point for the world, of course, and marked the emergence of the United States as a hegemonic superpower. But when I’ve covered this in the past, I consider everything from 1932 through 1968 to be part of “The Long Liberal Era”, with FDR and LBJ ushering in the New Deal and Great Society, respectively. Eisenhower was a notably moderate Republican, meanwhile, in an era of high bipartisan comity.

Applicability to 2026: If you follow politics, you’ll have a direct memory of some elections. The first one I remember watching — really just fragments, flickers of Reagan’s dominant map on the network newscasts — was in 1984. But the elections your parents remember will also be part of the “training set”: the collective memory that shapes conventional wisdom about how elections work. 1946 came before either of those, and that probably biases me against wanting to think it’s particularly relevant to today. You can draw some parallels: is the emergence of AI like the end of the war? And pent-up fatigue: Trump hasn’t had three terms in a row, but it feels like he has. Overall, this seems like a stretch.

1966 (12-point swing)

Outcome: Republicans gained 47 House seats and 3 Senate seats, although they failed to take control of either chamber; they also added 8 governorships, mostly west of the Mississippi.

When it happened: During LBJ’s second — but first elected — term. Like Truman, he therefore wasn’t a true lame duck, but dropped out of the 1968 race after a close call in the New Hampshire primary that was treated as a vote of no confidence.

Why it happened:

  • Increasing opposition to the Vietnam War on the left;

  • Increasing opposition to the Civil Rights movement and the hippies on the right;

  • Republicans were starting from a very, very low floor during a period in which they routinely got trounced in elections to Congress;

  • LBJ had brought sweeping changes to the welfare state.

What happened next? 1968 was competitive, with Hubert H. Humphrey nearly winning the popular vote, but Nixon was re-elected in a landslide in 1972. Overall, Republicans won the presidency in 5 of 6 elections, excepting only 1976.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Yes, I’d say: I think it was the precursor to the transition from the Long Liberal Era to the Long Conservative Era.

Applicability to 2026: Well, there’s a parallel in the form of a stupid war that nobody was asking for. And although LBJ wasn’t constitutionally a lame duck, he was on his back heel. But in other ways, the comparison is weaker. LBJ really did have an enormous mandate after his landslide in 1964, something that Trump never did.

1974 (11.2-point swing)

Outcome: Democrats gained 45 House seats, developing an enormous majority, along with 4 Senate seats and 4 governorships.

When it happened: Amid Gerald Ford’s lone (unelected) term after Nixon resigned the presidency in August 1974 following Watergate.

Why it happened: Watergate and inflation.

What happened next? A dark-horse Democratic nominee, Jimmy Carter, only narrowly beat Ford before losing in a landslide to Ronald Reagan in 1980 in an election that also produced massive gains in Congress for Republicans.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? No. Carter was not exactly transformational, and his presidency looks like a blip in the Long Conservative Era.

Applicability to 2026: People love this one, citing corruption and the high cost of living as parallels. And although Ford wasn’t a lame duck, Nixon had been and, like Trump, had been a central political figure for a long time, having been elected vice president in 1952. But I’d argue it’s only a medium-good comp. 1974 had a relatively singular cause, and scandals don’t bother the American public in the way they once did; corruption might have been only third on the list of voter concerns about Trump after high gas prices and Iran.

1994 (12.1-point swing)

Outcome: Republicans picked up 54 House seats, 8 Senate seats, and 10 governorships.

When it happened: In Bill Clinton’s first term, after he’d won in 1992 with a strong Electoral College performance but not a majority of the popular vote.

Why it happened:

  • The Clintons’ overreach on Hillarycare;

  • Bill Clinton’s personal scandals;

  • Although Clinton’s agenda wasn’t radical, we were in the midst of the Long Conservative Era;

  • Clinton had a tenuous mandate. Although he became popular following 1994, his first-term numbers more closely resembled the 43 percent of the vote he was elected with against George H.W. Bush and Ross Perot;

  • This was one of several elections (also 1972, 2010, 2016) that marked a series of step changes against Democrats in the rural South.

What happened next? Clinton performed a hard pivot to the center and was re-elected easily, although again without a popular-vote majority. His vice president, Al Gore, won the popular vote but lost the Electoral College to George W. Bush despite Clinton’s popularity and a strong economy.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? For me, no. Clinton was a centrist and triangulating president, which is why I see his presidency as being part of the Long Conservative Era.

Applicability to 2026: It’s a stretch. Clinton was in his first term, and although you can argue he overread his mandate, this ranks higher than most waves on structural explanations. The Democrats’ “Solid South” was falling apart and partisanship began a sharp rise under Newt Gingrich.

2006 (10.6 points)

Outcome: Democrats netted 31 House seats, flipped 6 Republican-held Senate seats (winning both chambers) and gained 6 governor’s mansions.

When it happened: In George Bush’s second, lame-duck term, following a close re-election in 2004.

Why it happened:

  • Bush’s ever-declining popularity amid fatigue with the War on Terror, his mishandling of Hurricane Katrina and his failed attempt at Social Security reform.

  • Bush governing as if he had a huge mandate when 2004 had been close.

  • Republican corruption and scandals.

  • Arguably, early warning signs of the mortgage bubble.

What happened next? Bush’s popularity continued to plummet; instead, the Republican nominee was John McCain, a Bush critic. But McCain nevertheless lost to Barack Obama by 7+ points, and Democrats had another huge year in Congress to rack up massive majorities in both chambers of Congress.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Clearly yes; I consider 2006 to be basically the end of the Long Conservative Era and the start of the New Liberal Era under Obama and later Biden.

Applicability to 2026: Obviously quite high. You had basically the same ingredients: unpopular wars, unforced errors, and looming economic anxiety. It’s also the only true lame duck midterm on the list. I’ve argued before that there are sharp parallels between 2004 and 2024, including the media being convinced that America was a “center-right country” despite the narrowness of the Bush and Trump wins. And take a look at this comparison between Bush and Trump’s second-term approval ratings:

2010 (17.4 points)

Outcome: Republicans hit the jackpot, picking up 6 Senate seats, 6 governorships, and 63 House seats.

When it happened: During Barack Obama’s first term, following his landslide win in 2008.

Why it happened:

  • The weak economic recovery following the global financial crisis and persistently high unemployment;

  • Democrats had a broad list of targets to defend after consecutive landslides in 2006 and 2008, with particular exposure in rural districts where the demographics were turning against them;

  • They had charged ahead to pass Obamacare even after losing a special Senate election in Massachusetts;

  • Populist backlash was brewing amid the rise of the Tea Party, which now reads like a precursor to Trumpism;

  • Obama’s penchant for turning out younger, low-propensity voters, particularly minorities, worked out well in presidential years but poorly in midterms.

What happened next? Obama, in a well-executed campaign, rebounded to soundly defeat Mitt Romney, picking up 2 Senate seats in the process to bolster the Democratic majority but failing to flip the House. A turnout/enthusiasm gap was again a problem for him in 2014 amidst a tepid economy, but he left office as a relatively popular president by modern standards. But then Democrats nominated Hillary Clinton, and then came Trump.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Not really. In some ways, it was kind of the reverse; this election was more of a market correction amid an emerging liberal era. Democrats would go on to win the popular vote for the U.S. presidency three more times in a row, with Obama’s vice president, Joe Biden, winning the Electoral College as a 77-year-old in 2020. But 2006/2008 only partly reflected a vibe shift involving changing cultural values on issues like gay marriage; there were also a lot of contingencies related to Bush, which didn’t have as much resonance once he was out of office, kept a low profile and tried his hand at painting.

Applicability to 2026: Strong in the sense that it’s the only swing of the same magnitude. But overall, relatively weak. Obama was in his first term, and had a far bigger mandate than Trump. Ironically, the parties have now swapped positions, and it was Trump who relied on low-propensity voters in his two Electoral College wins in 2016 and 2024 but has performed poorly in other elections.

So what can we learn from this?

Well, that’s not so straightforward.

Some experts have claimed that the predictive power of midterms is basically zero when forecasting forthcoming elections. (In fact, I’m guilty as charged; we published one such analysis at FiveThirtyEight.)

And it’s true that if you build a scatterplot of the magnitude of the midterm wave on the x-axis, and subsequent election results on the y-axis, it looks more or less random.

I have three critiques of this, though. One is a minor quibble: most midterms are waves, but analyses of elections like 2026 ought to focus on the ones that are similar in magnitude to it. With that said, there’s not much obvious signal: 2010 didn’t end up being all that bad for Barack Obama and Democrats, and even the public backlash to Watergate in 1974 didn’t persist for very long.

The second is that people tend to focus solely on the results of the next election two years later when long-term shifts are probably more important.

The main critique, however, is that these past midterm waves are very unlike one another. There are some common ingredients in play — overreaching one’s mandate, high exposure due to past success, dumb wars, etc. But the ratios are slightly different from election to election. In some cases, structural changes are a strong factor, and in others they don’t matter at all. In some years, like this one and in 1946, the president is extremely unpopular; in others, he’s only somewhat unpopular and the issue is more that there’s a relative decline from an election that brought large coattails.

The one crystal-clear parallel — I’d argue more than 1974 — is 2006, the only true lame-duck election on the list. That produced another landslide against Republicans two years later.

Am I just cherry-picking here? Yeah, kind of. Unfortunately, we sometimes have to do that in election analysis since we don’t get very many data points. I suppose my prior is that if we had 60 past elections instead of six, you would see some signal. But the point is, I think you’re allowed to be a little more qualitative when you don’t have enough reliable data points to fit a model anyway.

And one factor to consider is: how in the hell are Republicans going to go about picking an appealing candidate for 2028? JD Vance is the leader in prediction markets, but he’s Trump’s vice president. Marco Rubio, the other frontrunner, is the Secretary of State. I’m not sure there’s any John McCain looming on the horizon because it’s hard to be a McCain in Trump’s version of the Republican Party, which constantly excommunicates dissenters.

So really my argument is this. It seems unlikely to me that Trump’s approval rating, currently 38 percent, is liable to get all that much better. The decline in his numbers over the past two years has been remarkably persistent, instead. Plus, he’s 80 years old, and doesn’t seem to care about the implications of his unpopularity for anyone else in the Republican Party. I don’t think anyone is expecting him to attempt a Clintonian pivot, much less to pull it off. And the Republican nominee in 2028 will have to navigate an incredibly treacherous tightrope: distancing themselves just enough from Trump without triggering his ire. This produced a massive fail for Ron DeSantis last time around.

Until last night, you could at least argue that Trump’s low popularity was a mirage, a reflection of polls that weren’t capturing his real supporters. But not only did Republicans lose Senate seats in Texas (!) and South Carolina (!!) and Kansas (!!!) and maybe Mississippi (!!!!): Democrats were considerably underestimated by the polls. One theory for the polling miss, ironically, is that Trump is so unpopular that respondents won’t admit they once supported him, which can inflate Republican results in surveys that weight to past vote recall.

So, we’ll see. Democrats have plenty of their own problems, and last night didn’t erase them. We’re in an era when most presidential elections are close. I just don’t think you can witness last night without recognizing that Republicans are in a hell of a predicament. I’ll have more to say about this soon.

item.title: Models led prediction markets in forecasting the blue wave
item.description: But who deserves the most credit? High-quality pollsters who nailed the result. Plus, Still Counting EP10.
item.content:encoded:
Our weekly episode of Still Counting is ready. This was taped yesterday morning, so you can blame any bad takes on sleep deprivation:

And here’s the audio. We’re very grateful for any reviews, comments, likes and subscribes. Yes, I’m going to say that every week.

The context

Despite results on Tuesday that, to a first approximation, made our coverage this year look smart, Clare, Galen and I were all in slightly different moods. Elections build up to a stressful crescendo, frankly. It’s in the final days when you both have the most on the line and the most to do.

Subscribe now

And we’re still feeling that stress, to some extent. So rather than come up with the perfect transition paragraph, I’m going to semi-awkwardly pivot to a debate about models versus prediction markets.1

I don’t particularly like this debate. To a large extent, I think of pollsters, modelers, prediction markets and smart political wonks as all being within “the industry”. Their interests are mostly aligned with one another. And sometimes they’re aligned against the conventional wisdom or the media ecosystem more broadly.

If you’ve read the book, it’s kind of a Village vs. River thing. Or smart money vs. dumb money. The smart money was on Democrats having a good and possibly great election. The smart money doesn’t always get it right, though.

Still, I’m finding myself a little annoyed if prediction markets are trying to take a disproportionate share of the credit as opposed to “the industry” broadly. A few key points.

FLIPR was — correctly, given what happened — more confident in overall Democratic odds in the Senate throughout the stretch run of the campaign.2

For the Nov. 3 datapoint in this chart, I’m using the last “print” of prediction market data before any results were reported starting at 6 p.m. There was a weird little jitter back toward Republicans at prediction markets during the course of the day on Tuesday, which was directionally wrong and I don’t think had any real basis, as I wrote at the time. Prediction markets are smart about incorporating new information, and in principle that’s one of their advantages versus models — we have to wait for whatever happens to show up in the polls. At the same time, there’s sometimes a “buy the rumor, sell the news” thing going on here. Markets almost certainly overreacted to the Haley Stevens thing in Michigan and to random reports about turnout on Tuesday morning and afternoon.

Once results began to come in on Tuesday, prediction markets very, very quickly honed in on the right results. They were better than the networks, and faster than the NYT Needle. That was impressive, though I think we got to the right answer pretty quickly in the liveblog, too.

However, if we are going to turn this into a competition, I think the better models like FLIPR unambiguously had a better pre-election period. Our model arrived at the right answer faster, leading the markets by days to weeks.

Indeed, our forecasts moved the markets when they launched on Aug. 11. This is as clear an indication as you can get that traders believe we provide alpha that the markets alone are not capturing.

Furthermore, prediction market probabilities strongly converged toward ours in individual Senate and gubernatorial races. I was tracking this stuff closely, precisely because I envisioned that we might wind up in this sort of debate where prediction markets are low-key stealing valor from the models. I grabbed these prices late Tuesday morning. First for the Senate:

And then for gubernatorial races:

The differences are interesting. In the Nevada governor’s race, for instance, prediction markets were clearly incorporating some assumptions about early voting in correctly being more confident about Aaron Ford than we were. I think that was smart, although that’s partly because early-voting analysis tends to be unusually reliable in Nevada as compared to other states.

Sometimes, I have subjective takes that might override FLIPR, but we think projects like FLIPR are going to be more informative in the long run if we stick to the algorithm.

I am interested in the differences, however. I discussed the Senate races where prediction markets and FLIPR disagreed in a post on Oct. 25. The funny thing was, in several of the races like South Carolina, FLIPR was more accurate, but my “gut” was on the wrong side of FLIPR! Prediction markets do deserve some credit relative to FLIPR on Mississippi, though, where Scott Colom is probably going to win in a major upset.

Overall, though, prediction market prices converged toward FLIPR, and not the other way around. Here were the prices as of Oct. 25:

You can see that there were some bigger gaps then than we wound up with on Tuesday. Although, the correlation was >=.99 in both cases.

You can also debate how to compare them. If Peltola wins in Alaska but by an underwhelming margin, as seems likely, does FLIPR deserve credit for showing a closer race? Or not, because prediction markets also “called” the right winner, but did so more confidently? Any evaluation that anyone publishes is usually going to be low-key biased toward the most favorable “reasonable” method for their forecast.

In the end, prediction markets and the better models converged on basically the same prices. But as you can see by comparing the Oct. 25 graphic to the Nov. 3 graphic, prediction markets moved toward model prices and not the other way around. The prices they wound up with on Tuesday morning, we often had days to weeks sooner.

I don’t want to turn this into a competition between Silver Bulletin and the other models. Split Ticket and FiftyPlusOne in particular also have smart models. (There’s more or less a “right” way to build one of these, so we all use pretty similar approaches.) Different analyses put their performance in slightly different orders. Yes, there were one or two other models that I thought were slightly wacky, but in general, these differences have dissipated, and the modeling part of “the industry” has matured from, say, 2016.

But traders get to use our forecasts, and they trust them, and I’m sure they make up some proportion of our subscription business.

The best-performing models, including FLIPR, don’t use prediction market data, however. They provide truly independent information. If there aren’t reliable models to look at, prediction markets are still often smart. But they can also get unhinged, like in the Wisconsin and Michigan Democratic primaries this year.

Building these models is a lot of work, with some subtle dynamics that take a lot of time to explore fully. One of those, for instance, is that polling in primaries is much less accurate than polls of general elections. So the markets sometimes wind up trusting polls too much in primaries, and too little in general elections.

It’s flattering that traders tend to trust our prices. But in a world where these models didn’t exist, or if the models kept their forecasts private, I don’t think the prediction markets would be as accurate on either an absolute or relative basis.

However, there’s an irony here. Just like the prediction markets are downstream of the models and benefit from their existence, the models are downstream from the inputs they use, including the polls. If you ask me, who really deserves the most credit is pollsters like NYT/Siena and AtlasIntel that provided highly accurate results that defied the consensus to some degree. There would have been hell to pay if these polls had been off, especially given that the president has sued pollsters before that he didn’t like. It showed some courage for them to stick their necks out there and they deserve a victory lap.

So if I had to rank-order this, I’d go something like:

1) NYT, AtlasIntel and other high-quality pollsters who trusted their own data and published their results at some risk of embarrassment.

Close 2nd) The better models, including but not limited to FLIPR.

Close 3rd) Prediction markets. They did have a good year, certainly. And I think it shows them maturing that they increasingly trust the more reliable sources of information and shut out the noise.

Distant 4th) The conventional wisdom, more broadly, which incorrectly assumed that polls are persistently biased against Republicans. They aren’t. Polling bias is basically random from cycle to cycle, in part because pollsters adjust their methods in response to errors. This election wasn’t the first time that polls missed low on Democrats. The same thing happened in the New Jersey and Virginia gubernatorial races last year, and in the presidential election of 2012.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

  • Clare, Galen and I will be at Crooked Con in Washington D.C. this weekend, with a live Still Counting episode at 9 a.m. on Saturday!

  • The post-election period can be tricky. As discussed yesterday, we’re going to look to strike a balance between reflections on the midterm, more forward-looking coverage, and posts that have nothing to do with the election at all. We have a big year planned, including one or two new sports model launches. We also need to get some rest.

To receive new posts and support our work, please consider becoming a subscriber.

1

I’m an advisor to Polymarket. But my first priority is always the newsletter, and saying what I think, including when prediction markets get things wrong.

2

And to a lesser extent in the House, although everyone was highly confident throughout.

item.title: The most valuable nomination of all time?
item.description: On Still Counting EP11, we talked about Jon Ossoff and the bright but uncertain future for Democrats.
item.content:encoded:
Ironically, because Washington is so close to New York, I don’t really see much of the city. It’s not like going to LA where, even on a work trip, I’ll plan some excursions — it’s pretty much in and out. But I did get to spend some time on Saturday, on a crisp afternoon, walking and running along the National Mall. The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool looks great, by the way; the White House does not.

I was also in DC for the 2008 presidential election, and of course there were lots of celebrations even in a famously buttoned-up town. Midterms aren’t like that and don’t trigger the same outpouring of emotions (except maybe, this year, in Austin). And that’s fairly rational, I suppose. Republicans have nothing at all to celebrate, except maybe Florida and some comparative overperformance in New England. But for Democrats, the job is only half-done. Even with large majorities in the House and Senate, Congress will serve as less of a check on a president’s power when he exercises most of his authority through executive actions anyway — and the powers of the executive branch are interpreted liberally by courts. The 2026 midterm will go down in the history books, and the election was played for keeps. Democrats will probably hold the Senate even if they lose the presidential race in two years. But the total and complete repudiation of Trump that Democrats are hoping for will require flipping the White House in 2028, too.

So in our Still Counting live show in Washington on Saturday, we talked about what the future holds for Democrats:

Audio version here. As always, we’re grateful for any reviews, comments, likes and subscribes. Note that this was taped in front of a live audience.

The context

You can accuse us of pandering to the crowd, but Galen, Clare, and I conducted a “mini-draft” of Democratic primary candidates. The truth is, it didn’t differ that much from our last pre-midterm draft. But this time, I was lucky enough to draw the first pick and chose who is technically the senior Senator from Georgia, Jon Ossoff. I selected his colleague Raphael Warnock with my second pick, and Gavin Newsom in the third round. (I’m not a fan of the latter exactly, but I’ll grab value when I see it.)

At prediction markets, Ossoff is now the frontrunner by some margin, with about a 1-in-4 chance of becoming the nominee — AOC is second — although traders are also not necessarily convinced that he’ll run.

Subscribe now

There’s perhaps a little bit of a syndrome here of Ossoff having become the consensus #1 overall NBA/NFL pick with a degree of projection involved. I was going to write something about how he hasn’t really “proven” anything, but that’s inherently true for basically any potential presidential nominee. And this is not exactly a “stats vs. scouts” thing. Ossoff won Georgia by 18 points on Tuesday. Sure, in baseball terms, you can “park-adjust” that result; it was an extremely favorable climate for Democrats, who are going to win the national House popular vote by something like 13 or 14 points. He hit .370, but it was at the equivalent of Coors Field.

It was nevertheless an impressive outcome. And the man’s talents are pretty obvious. In particular, Ossoff seems roughly equally acceptable to both the moderate and progressive factions of the Democratic Party. That’s how nominations are typically won in the Democratic Party (although it hasn’t always resulted in great candidates). Ossoff easily won the Crooked Con straw poll, which, for what it’s worth, probably reflects a reasonably fair balance between the progressive and moderate factions of the Democratic Party.

Ossoff also said during the closing weeks of his campaign that he won’t run in 2028. These sorts of protestations aren’t very reliable, however. Politicians, notably including Ossoff, have big egos. He doesn’t even have the excuse anymore of potentially being replaced in the Senate by a Republican, since Keisha Lance Bottoms will become Georgia’s new governor in January.

Do I buy that he might not run? Sure, I guess. Who knows what’s in anybody’s heart. Mostly, though, I presume that people respond fairly rationally to incentives. And the 2028 Democratic nomination is an extremely desirable one, for three reasons.

  1. The “fundamentals” are strong for Democrats.

At prediction markets, Democrats are roughly 2-to-1 favorites to win in 2028.

This is a slightly uncomfortable fact. 2-to-1 is a pretty bold forecast; it’s not 55/45 or 60/40. The heuristic that presidential elections should basically default to a toss-up in the absence of polls or other information is usually hard to beat. On top of that — and we’ve been guilty of this ourselves sometimes — there can be a tendency to project forward from the most recent election result, when the boring bet of mean reversion is usually more reliable in the long run. Presidential elections in the modern American system are typically highly competitive. It’s easy to imagine any number of ways in which things could go poorly for Democrats, including by choosing a “bad” nominee.

I’m not sure I want this to turn into the official “does Nate really think Democrats are 2:1 favorites in 2028 given current conditions?” post. I need to think more about it. For instance, I want to think about Democrats’ state-by-state performance and consider whether that implies any sort of Electoral College disadvantage — or perhaps even an advantage. One of the few bright spots for Kamala Harris in 2024 was that the Electoral College/popular vote gap closed significantly. She lost the tipping-point state, Pennsylvania, by 1.7 points, essentially the same as her 1.5-point overall loss to Trump in the national popular vote. Part of that was because Democrats’ biggest declines, and Trump’s biggest gains, came in places like New York City where Democrats can afford to hemorrhage voters because they’ll win still by humongous margins instead of spectacularly humongous ones. In a Moneyball sense, that makes for a more efficient coalition, since you don’t have quite as many wasted votes.

Still, I’ve probably already tipped my hand on this question. I think the 2006/2008 precedent is quite relevant. Among the famous recent-ish midterm landslides, only 2006 featured a true lame-duck president. And the election two years later went about as well as possible for Democrats; Barack Obama even won Indiana.

It’s not necessarily impossible to imagine President Trump becoming a bit more popular by 2028, particularly if partisan motivated reasoning kicks in. But it is hard to see him becoming outright popular, especially since the internals on his approval ratings — only 20 percent of Americans strongly approve of the president’s performance — are actually worse than the headline numbers. It’s also hard to imagine the Republican nominee in 2028 fully distancing himself from Trump’s shadow.

Still, there are very likely to be wild twists and turns that nobody anticipates.

But at the very least, 2028 is a highly winnable election for Democrats. If you’re on the fence between running and not running, there might not be a better opportunity any time soon.

  1. If Democrats win the presidency, the president will probably command fairly large congressional majorities.

We covered the 2028 Senate outlook in Friday’s newsletter. Democrats are probably going to wind up with 56 Senate seats this year. It would likely take a Republican landslide in 2028 to reverse that majority in the span of a single election.

Humility would say not to rule a GOP landslide out, but I think that’s a less likely outcome than a narrow GOP win, a narrow Democratic win, or a D landslide. Even under a 2024-like scenario, Democrats would probably hold their Senate majority. And in the latter two scenarios, they might expand it.

The House is a different question. In the Senate, two-thirds of the seats hold over from year to year. Maybe FLIPR will annoy our bluer subscribers that year, but look, 2032 might be a rough year for Democrats, and incumbents like Scott Colom in Mississippi are going to be extremely vulnerable. But that’s six years away and, presuming Colom is eventually declared the winner, he’s earned his Senate seat until then.

In the House, everyone comes up for election every two years, however. What long-term gains do you lock in by winning? Not necessarily that many, although there are some.

The incumbency advantage, however diminished it is, is probably still a net-positive: you can look at an election like 2012 when Obama had a pretty great year but Democrats didn’t come particularly close to flipping back the House after their disaster in 2010. The other long-term benefit would be to lock in some gains from redistricting, which is now an every-two-years thing instead of once a decade.

I’m not sure I’ve fully processed the implications of 2026 for state legislatures and so forth, other than that they’re obviously directionally favorable for Democrats. It’s not strictly impossible that Democrats win the presidency by say 1 point in 2028 but lose control of the House; that would be one of those FLIPR-ish outcomes that nobody necessarily “buys”. Nevertheless, a trifecta is likely if not certain conditional upon a Democrat winning the presidency.

  1. The opportunity to define the Democratic Party

To a first approximation, one might say that American political parties are defined through presidential nominations. But there are times when the parameters are a little more open, and this looks like one of those years on the Democratic side.

Isn’t 2028 going to be an existential nomination for the GOP too? Trumpism/MAGA versus some Whole New Thing is as existential as it gets. I’m just not sure how easy it will be to create the Whole New Thing by 2028. A “45-degree pivot from MAGA” seems like the game-theory equilibrium. That might produce a little bit of a “lipstick-on-a-pig” nomination for Republicans when it takes until 2032 for the party to rid itself of Trumpism.

Still, the Democratic Party is fairly leaderless and rudderless at the moment. In a weird way, that might have been an advantage last Tuesday. The party basically nominated a bunch of normal-seeming people who were reasonably well-curated for their local environments, while Republicans didn’t. In presidential years, though, you have to stand for something, not just against something. It’s not obvious what Democrats stand for exactly, but the 2028 nominee is going to have a lot to say about that.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

The pace of newsletters is going to slow down soon enough, though we’re not done reflecting on 2026. I’m also thinking it might be a good time for our much-belated update to our Jan. 2025 post, 113 predictions for Trump’s second term.

I also don’t want to wait too long before digging in on our next big modeling project, rebooting our NBA projection system, a.k.a. RAPTOR 2.0.

And we’re probably going to be posting a job listing or two soon. Look, we’re always amazed by how much support we get from you subscribers and feel incredibly lucky and privileged for it. We think it makes sense to continue investing in the product to hopefully give you an even better and more robust Silver Bulletin experience. We’re not quite sure about how we want to go about doing this, but we figure Silver Bulletin has probably grown out of the “three kids in a trench coat + an NCAA tournament model” stage.

item.title: JD Vance and the VP curse
item.description: If you’re the VP to an unpopular president, the rest of your career usually doesn’t go well. Plus, a post-midterm Republican primary draft on Still Counting EP12.
item.content:encoded:
We’re back to our regular schedule for Still Counting after taping bonus episodes last week and this weekend.1 So this is our regular Wednesday episode. After considering how the extraordinary midterm landslide might affect Democrats’ 2028 plans, we turned to Republicans this time.

Audio version here. Your reviews, comments, likes and subscribes are always appreciated.

The context

I won’t speak for Galen and Clare, but I found drafting the Republicans less fun than the Democrats. That’s partly because the field is top-heavy. The top three Republican contenders, deemed by prediction markets to be JD Vance, Marco Rubio and Ron DeSantis, together have about a two-thirds chance of being the nominee, leaving little win probability for anyone else.

You could argue that’s miscalibrated, though for better or worse, it roughly tracks polls — which are more predictive than you might assume even at this stage — where Vance and Rubio are way ahead of anyone else, including DeSantis.

But Vance’s odds have plummeted since Labor Day, when Democrats began to surge in midterm polls. I don’t think prediction market traders get everything right, but the notion that a bad midterm result for Trump might encourage voters to look beyond the vice president for a successor seems sound enough.

DeSantis has been the biggest recent riser, meanwhile. I guess the thinking here is that he’s still MAGA-y enough to get away with criticizing Republicans while offering some degree of proven electoral performance and not being directly tied to the deeply unpopular administration. His poor performance in the 2024 nomination race raises the question of whether his 2022 popularity surge was an artifact of COVID plus the fact that Florida has now become really red. Overall, though, the field has opened up, with Vance and Rubio going from a 70 percent combined chance of being the nominee to just under 50 percent now.

Subscribe now

But I’m not here to talk about DeSantis or the rest of the field. Instead, let’s consider the vice president, whom we’ve sparsely covered at Silver Bulletin. Vance issued his own election post-mortem, which placed almost all of the blame directly or indirectly on the Iran War, where he’s made his disagreements with Trump known through frequent leaks to the press.

Some conservatives have started to question whether Vance should even run in 2028. Unlike the Democratic nomination, the GOP nod in two years is perhaps not all that desirable. Unless President Trump’s dismal approval ratings improve, the election figures to be an uphill battle for Republicans. Meanwhile, the filtering effect of having to implicitly or explicitly receive Trump’s seal of approval has squashed intellectual diversity in the party. You can name the exceptions — successful non-MAGA Republicans, like Brian Kemp in Georgia, Kelly Ayotte in New Hampshire, and Spencer Cox in Utah — on one hand. And most of them probably aren’t prominent enough or conservative enough to make a serious bid.2

Trump’s situation could improve. Recent political history is full of examples where the conventional wisdom over-extrapolated from the results of a single election. Trump himself has made big comebacks too, returning to the presidency four years after being impeached for the second time. Gas prices might decline, the war might end, and Democrats have nominated a series of C-tier presidential nominees lately.

But consider the headlines from this week:

  • Republicans had to fend off an impeachment attempt against Pete Hegseth led by the outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie;

  • An interest-rate hike has become highly likely after a hot inflation report;

  • Nvidia CEO and Trump ally Jensen Huang stepped down after acknowledging infidelity amid reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The New York Times also reported an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.

  • Trump replaced Susie Wiles as chief of staff with Stephen Miller, who is associated with the hardline immigration policies that even the most moderate Democrats successfully campaigned against last week.

  • And Scott Colom was declared the winner in Mississippi.

Plus, Trump is 80 years old, the point at which visible signs of Joe Biden’s age-related decline really started to accelerate. Meanwhile, Republicans have consistently struggled to win elections during the Trump Era when Trump himself wasn’t on the ballot, and he’s notorious for not really caring much about the fate of other Republicans.

Could Vance succeed at distancing himself from Trump on Iran or other issues? Disagreements between the president and the vice president were common until recently. Before the passage of the 12th Amendment in 1804, a rivalry was unavoidable because the second-place finisher in the presidential race became the vice president. (Imagine if Kamala Harris were still VP today, but under Trump.) In 1832, John Calhoun actually resigned the vice presidency because of his differences with Andrew Jackson. One of FDR’s vice presidents, John Nance Garner, ran against him for the 1940 nomination. LBJ bitterly feuded with the Kennedys (mostly Bobby). And more recently, rioters at the Capitol during the Jan. 6 insurrection chanted “Hang Mike Pence” after Pence refused to interrupt the certification of Biden’s win in 2020.

The modern level of high partisan loyalty makes it harder for vice presidents to distance themselves from their boss’s policies, however. Harris completely failed to differentiate herself from Biden, and didn’t even try. Trump’s tendency to punish dissent puts Vance in a box, meanwhile.

Nor had Vance particularly been a strong electoral performer. Prior to winning the vice presidency, his only previous bid for office came in 2022, when he won Ohio’s Senate race by 6 points but underperformed Ohio’s Republican governor, Mike DeWine, who won re-election by 25 points instead.

There’s also another unfavorable trend for Vance. In recent years, while vice presidents to unpopular presidents have frequently won their party’s nominations, they’ve developed a poor track record in general elections. There basically isn’t any good example since presidential approval ratings began of the VP to an unpopular president later being elected president himself.

Let’s run back the tape to the mid-1960s, considering every vice president since Humphrey. I figure this is the relevant dataset because it coincides with the development of the modern presidential nomination system, which emerged over roughly 1968-1980 and gave voters more say in the process.

Hubert H. Humphrey (1965-1969 under Lyndon Baines Johnson)

LBJ was initially on track to seek a second elected term, but bowed out after only getting 49.6 percent of the vote, as a write-in candidate, against Eugene McCarthy in the New Hampshire primary, a watershed moment for popular participation mattering in the nomination process. However, Humphrey eventually received the nomination over the anti-war McCarthy at the Democrats’ infamous and violent 1968 convention in Chicago. Despite the problems in Chicago, Humphrey only barely lost the popular vote to Richard Nixon, but Nixon’s Electoral College margin was sound (the populist, segregationist George Wallace received 46 electoral votes). Humphrey sought the 1972 nomination, but lost to the left-wing George McGovern, who benefited from having helped to design the rules of the new nomination system.

Spiro Agnew (1969-1973 under Richard Nixon)

Agnew resigned the vice presidency amid a bribery scandal unrelated to Watergate nine months into Nixon’s second term and never ran for office again.

Gerald Ford (1973-1974 under Richard Nixon)

Ford ascended to the presidency after Nixon’s resignation and won a highly contentious 1976 nomination as an unelected incumbent against Ronald Reagan. But Ford lost the November election to Jimmy Carter. (Although as with Humphrey in 1968, it was closer than you might expect under the circumstances.) Ford did not appear on an election ballot again, but made a play to be Reagan’s running mate at the GOP convention in 1980.

Nelson Rockefeller (1974-1977 under Gerald Ford)

After a fairly distinguished career with four terms as governor of New York, Rockefeller was 68 years old at the time his vice presidency tenure ended and his moderation was out of step with the Reagan Revolution. He died two years later.

Walter Mondale (1977-1981 under Jimmy Carter)

Mondale won the Democratic nomination in 1984 in a contentious race against Gary Hart and Jesse Jackson, and then lost in a landslide to Reagan. So this is one of the better examples of it being hard to escape the shadow of an unpopular president, even if you wait four years to run yourself. Mondale became Paul Wellstone’s replacement in the 2002 Minnesota Senate race after Wellstone died in a plane crash, but lost by 2 points to Norm Coleman.

George H.W. Bush (1981-1989 under Ronald Reagan)

Bush Sr. claimed the 1988 GOP nomination after an initial stumble in Iowa and was elected easily over Michael Dukakis — though Dukakis had led for parts of the race — producing a third consecutive Republican term. His popularity skyrocketed after the Gulf War but plummeted just as the economy struggled to recover from a recession and high inflation. He faced growing strains of populism — Pat Buchanan within the Republican Party, Ross Perot — before losing to Bill Clinton in an election in which he got only 37.5 percent of the popular vote.

Dan Quayle (1989-1993 under George H.W. Bush)

Always considered a lightweight, Quayle skipped the 1996 race and made an all-in play for Iowa during the 2000 Republican nomination, where he was running against Bush Jr., but withdrew in September 1999 after making no traction in the polls.

Al Gore (1993-2001 under Bill Clinton)

Gore swept all 50 states in winning the 2000 nomination over Bill Bradley, but lost the Electoral College to Bush Jr. by 537 votes following a recount in Florida (that was halted by the Supreme Court). He remained a reasonably prominent public figure for some time, focusing on the environment, but hasn’t sought public office again.

Dick Cheney (2001-2009 under George W. Bush)

Never considered to have presidential ambitions on his own, Cheney didn’t run in 2008, depriving us of a data point from one of the better precedents for Trump’s second term.

Joe Biden (2009-2017 under Barack Obama)

Chosen by Obama in part because Obama considered him too old to run for president himself3, Biden seriously considered running in 2016 but ceded to Hillary Clinton. He did seek the 2020 nomination at age 76, where he was treated as an underdog by many pundits despite always polling strongly, then boomeranged to win after strong showings in South Carolina and on Super Tuesday. The nomination race that year was one of the clearest examples of a party putting a finger on the scale, with a series of endorsements for Biden as trepidation about a Bernie Sanders nomination and the COVID pandemic motivated the party to rally behind the perceived safer choice. Biden defeated Trump that November, though in an election that was closer than polls projected.

Buoyed by a comparatively strong showing by Democrats in the 2022 midterm, Biden sought a second term when many Democrats assumed he wouldn’t. Amid supermajorities of voters expressing concerns about his age, he fared disastrously at a June 2024 debate against Trump, and eventually stood down after a power struggle, while making it clear that Harris was his second choice.

Mike Pence (2017-2021 under Donald Trump)

A fairly conventional vice president in one of Trump’s more orthodox campaign decisions, Pence refused to prevent the certification of the 2020 presidential vote under pressure from Trump and protesters at the Jan. 6 insurrection. He sought the 2024 nomination but rarely escaped the single digits in polls. Pence refused to endorse Trump in the November general election.

Kamala Harris (2021-2025 under Joe Biden)

Chosen by Biden as his running mate in 2020 despite flopping in the Democratic nomination race and exiting early, in part because of identity politics dynamics within the party, Harris was given a challenging portfolio by Biden in a way that possibly undermined her ability to develop star power of her own and become the logical “bridge” after a caretaker term. Replacing Biden in July 2024 after 25 days of intensive drama, Harris hit the ground running and initially gained momentum amid Brat Summer, but was unable or unwilling to sufficiently distance herself from Biden and had trouble defining a clear brand or lane for herself. She lost to Trump in November in an election that was closer than the mandate it was sometimes interpreted as being. Still, she was the first Democrat since 2004 to lose the popular vote and underperformed Democratic Senate candidates in key states. She is reportedly considering running again in 2028.

JD Vance (2025- under Donald Trump)

So this starts to look like a pretty bad track record for Vance.

Which other vice presidents sought the presidency after serving under presidents who were unpopular near the end of their presidencies4? Bush, Biden and Gore don’t count because Reagan, Obama and Clinton were reasonably popular as of the end of their terms.5

Humphrey lost. Ford lost. Mondale lost in a landslide. Quayle and Pence had no hope of winning their nominations. Harris lost, narrowly.

Among the VPs to relatively popular presidents, Gore lost too. Biden won after a four-year hiatus but is likely to be remembered by history as having held on too long in seeking a second term. H.W. Bush is the clearest success story but, like Biden, was a one-termer.

Sure, a couple of those elections — Gore’s certainly — might have gone the other way. But in recent years, we’ve added Harris and Pence as failures. And if you ask me, Biden looks like a cautionary tale too.

Maybe this is a case of just not enough data to make for reliable extrapolations. We’re talking about nine examples here, not dozens. And some of them are only partial failures.

And as I said, VPs have good track records of winning party nominations; it’s general elections that have been the trouble spot.

But that may partly reflect power vacuums within their parties. Just like someone has to be the Minnesota Vikings’ quarterback, someone has to win the Republican nomination in two years.

But parties with lame-duck presidents are often stuck between a rock and a hard place. The existing president is term-limited — or too old or unpopular to run again. Meanwhile, he’ll often have squashed or discredited opposition in his party. And presidents usually have poor midterms that deprive the party of fresh prospects. So the bill comes due, and the honor of paying it often defaults to the veep. But it’s not the sort of check that candidates are necessarily lining up to pay.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

We’ve updated ELWAY with trades as of Tuesday’s deadline. We hope to increase the amount of sports coverage soon, but in the meantime we’re now typically updating ELWAY and QBERT three times a week.

We’ll take a couple of weeks off around the holidays. Honestly, we need it because we expect the nomination races to get going quickly — and for Trump to create plenty of other news in the meantime.

2

Or in the case of Florida Governor-elect Byron Donalds, my 3rd-round pick, they’re too new in office. There’s no constitutional problem for Donalds, but candidates rarely immediately turn around and run for president after winning a major statewide office for the first time. (I’m not sure whether I’d classify Donalds as MAGA.)

3

Though I’ll note that the reporting on this claim is a bit speculative; there’s no definitive account of it.

4

This phrasing is intentional; presidents sometimes get a sort of sympathy/reverse-honeymoon approval rating bounce toward the very end of their terms once their parties have lost the election or are transitioning out of power.

5

Although to varying degrees, they experienced approval-rating slumps in the middle of their terms.

item.title: Fighters vs. uniters and the big blue future
item.description: The Democratic base is in a fighting mood. But Democrats now have a bigger tent to hold together.
item.content:encoded:
As you may know, I’m fond of finding different ways to classify Democrats. Usually, this concerns the party’s voters, but in a New York Times story out this morning, I turned to their candidates.

I have no problem with dividing the candidates into progressives and moderate “lanes,” particularly if one recognizes it as a spectrum rather than a strict boundary. But after spending a bunch of time last week binge-watching videos, debates, press appearances, and ads from 27 Democratic candidates — 13 leading 2028 contenders, plus 13 candidates who made major breakthroughs on Nov. 31, plus Zohran Mamdani2 — I don’t think that really captures the whole story.

Instead, there’s another distinction that I call “fighter” vs. “uniter.”

It really does help to watch the candidates in action to see this. Some classifications are obvious. Gavin Newsom’s whole thing is to fight back by any means necessary. When it came to leading Democratic efforts to fight Republican redistricting, I thought that was smart. I could do without his Trump-style tweeting, but I can understand why some voters like it.

While “fighter” is correlated with “progressive,” the relationship is far from perfect. I consider Zohran to be a hybrid of “fighter” and “uniter,” but he’s closer to the latter end of the spectrum and often finds a way to signal that he wants to be a mayor for all New Yorkers, including through his consummately well-presented appearance.

Conversely, I expected Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear to be fairly mild-mannered, and he often is, but look at him talking about JD Vance:

There were a lot of cases like this. I classified only Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton as a pure uniter, a 7 on my 7-point scale. But you can watch someone like Mary Peltola get more and more worked up in her Oct. 15 debate against Dan Sullivan, for instance. In her opening statement, she described herself affably as a “lifelong Alaskan, a mother, a grandmother” — but by 10 minutes in, she’d gotten under his skin — and him under hers. “Dan, you should be ashamed of yourself for propagating these lies,” she said.

Subscribe now

I don’t want to preempt the NYT story too much, so go check it out. An undercurrent is simply how skilled some of the Class of 2026 are at communication. While James Talarico is perhaps the most obvious example of someone who can blend “fighter” and “uniter” styles, you’re seeing a lot of creative ways to bridge the gap, from Scott Colom’s use of humor to South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews playing the “I’m just a working mom and pediatrician” card in one commercial to some incredibly vicious attacks on the late Lindsey Graham (when he was originally her opponent) in another.

Why “uniter” may be a more natural gear for Democrats

One thing I talked through with my editor, but we didn’t really have space to fit into the piece, is whether one strategy is likely to be more correlated with winning, either in the general election or the primary.

I thought it was clear enough that the 2028 candidates (or their consultants) are mostly moving in the fighter direction. In recent speeches, Jon Ossoff’s rhetoric has been extremely sharp and unforgiving toward Republicans. He still has something of an Obama-esque cadence, but unlike most of the other candidates who are accused of this (Pete Buttigieg, Josh Shapiro, Wes Moore) he doesn’t tilt toward the “uniter” end of the scale. His rhetoric was more like Newsom’s instead.

Obama’s shadow does loom over the field, however. His 2008 primary battle against Hillary Clinton was a pretty good example of “fighter” vs. “uniter,” and the uniter won — and then went on to capture 365 electoral votes that November.

Nor, despite nearly all Democrats saying they want to fight back harder against Trump in polls, does that necessarily match Democrats’ revealed preferences in primaries. Talarico’s win over Jasmine Crockett was a strike against Team Fighter, for instance.

And there’s an asymmetry between the parties that might make the “uniter” style more natural for Democrats.

Here’s a crazy stat I came across the other day. Since 2008, Democrats have won a Senate race in 43 states. Kansas, Maine3, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas were added to the list this year.

This includes 13 states where Democrats haven’t won an electoral vote any time this century. Here is the same map for Republicans:

Visually, it still looks fairly impressive thanks to the presence of all those big square states in the middle of the country. But the GOP map is much patchier, with 15 states missing4 including the entire West Coast and most of the Northeast. Moreover, there’s a much closer overlap between where the GOP wins Senate seats and where they’re competitive in the presidency.

Classically in American politics, Democrats are the “big tent” coalition. They were the party of manual laborers, but also college professors, Black voters and most immigrant groups. Throughout almost all of recent American history, Democrats have led Republicans in party identification — though their lead used to be much larger before the Solid South turned red. (Although the South wasn’t so red this year.)

But, obviously, it’s not as though Democrats have monopolized American politics during this time. Since Jan. 1, 1940, through today, Democrats have controlled the presidency 52 percent of the time, about as close to even as it gets.

However, they’ve controlled the Senate 67 percent of the time and the House 68 percent during the same period. A lot of that came during the Solid South era of conservative, Southern Democrats. Still, the final two years of Trump’s term will widen that president vs. Congress gap. In some ways, it’s a throwback.

What accounts for the difference? Well, some of it is that Democrats’ breadth and diversity is more of a strength when they can curate candidates for individual states and districts instead of having to pick one for the whole country. With one or two exceptions5, the Democrats who won big on Nov. 3, from El-Sayed to Peltola to Colom, were very distinctively products of their respective states.

So the question is: while everyone likes a fighter, who or what are they fighting for, exactly? El-Sayed is a “fighter,” but so, unquestionably, was Haley Stevens.

Even the red state Democrats who won this year spoke with plenty of fire and conviction about high prices, about corruption, and against billionaires like Elon Musk. Those are likely to be winning themes in the presidential nomination as well as being advantages for Democrats in November 2028. Some of those same Democrats, though — like Gina Hinojosa, who actually has a fairly progressive record in the Texas state legislature — were going out of their way to reject the “culture wars.” Some featured Trump prominently but others did not — and this is trickier than you might think to navigate for 2028 since Trump himself won’t be on the ballot.

Plus, the Democratic Party has a lot of racial, class, age, religious and gender differences to bridge. (You don’t have to be woke to recognize that how candidates are perceived by voters is mediated by their race, gender and appearance.6) Sometimes, the Democrats who are urging “fight, fight, fight” can mistake the party’s online, liberal/progressive activist base for the broader base that the party really needs to win, including voters of color and many churchgoing Americans.

So I’ll cast a tentative vote for “uniter” being slightly underrated. Either way, though, go watch some of these candidates in action, especially the Class of 2026. Moving past the era of the Clintons and the Bidens and the Cuomos and even the Janet Millses has opened up space for Democrats who are far more modern and effective communicators. Democrats really do have a lot of talent on their hands.

1

No, there isn’t much overlap between these groups. It’s very rare for someone to win a major statewide office for the first time and then immediately turn around to run for president.

2

Zohran is not in the “Class of 2026” since he was elected mayor last year, and he’s not a 2028 contender since he’s a naturalized citizen and therefore isn’t eligible to be president.

3

If you don’t count Angus King, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats.

4

15 includes Michigan, which Trump won twice but where Republicans haven’t elected a Senator any time recently.

5

Annie Andrews struck me as someone who was speaking to more of a national audience, although that may be partly because she was making appeals for donor money.

6

As I said in the NYT story, there are a conspicuously large number of good-looking Democrats among the party’s rising stars.

item.title: Silver Bulletin is hiring an editor and a developer
item.content:encoded:
Silver Bulletin is hiring a Deputy Editor and an Associate Interactive Developer.

The Deputy Editor is a full-time role for someone with editing experience in journalism or a closely related field and a strong interest in our major beats, which include politics (especially elections), sports, and AI.

We envision the Associate Interactive Developer role as initially part-time and open to candidates early in their careers. We would consider a full-time and/or more experienced hire for an exceptional candidate who can persuade us of the value they’d bring to the site.

The deadline to apply for both positions is 5 p.m. ET on Friday, December 18. We’ll begin reviewing materials and interviewing candidates in early January and don’t expect to contact applicants before the deadline. Interviews will be conducted by video or in person.

Even if the jobs aren’t a good fit for you, we’d encourage you to circulate these listings to people who might be interested. Silver Bulletin is an equal opportunity employer. We welcome applicants from all backgrounds provided they are eligible to work in the United States.

Silver Bulletin is growing as a business and maturing as a site. Our newsletters and models typically reach hundreds of thousands to millions of readers. The economics of the business are sound, and we hope these will be long-term roles with growth potential for ambitious candidates.

We want to make our coverage more robust, improving both quality and quantity in the areas where our subscribers already really like our coverage. We’re looking for hires who have opinions about the strengths and shortcomings of the site and ideas about how to make it better. Our current four-person team works incredibly hard, but we’re overstretched. We want a couple of new voices in the room to help us do more for our readers.

We use AI tools for tasks such as copy editing and helping code our models, but writing at Silver Bulletin is done by human hands. Beyond assistance with standard copy editing and formatting, you should disclose any use of AI in completing your application.

Deputy Editor

The Deputy Editor job requires strong people skills and an understanding of both our journalism and our business. Although this isn’t the only metric for success, we’d like to publish about one additional high-quality story per week.

Job tasks

  • Edit work from Silver Bulletin staff and freelancers. This will often include “nose-to-tail” editing: working with the writers to develop the story, sharpen the argument, and improve the precision of the published piece.

  • Help develop our editorial plan from day to day and week to week. Plan around the demands of the news cycle, weighing the trade-offs between responsiveness and depth.

  • Develop a group of paid freelancers to add coverage on our main beats, with a particular emphasis on building out our AI coverage. Consider logical areas for expansion, such as economics, finance, tech, and public policy.

  • Serve as a sounding board for the overall direction of the newsletter and provide another set of eyes when we’re publishing stories on sensitive topics. Help mentor staff and freelancers.

  • Develop and enforce a style guide and editorial standards, including standards for the use of AI. Be the point person for correcting typographical and factual errors, including in our graphics and statistical models.

  • Plan and populate the Silver Bulletin homepage, review audience analytics, and assist with headlines, graphics, and the visual appearance of the site.

  • Help organize coverage of major events, including liveblogs and live events.

  • Help with photo selection, fair-use questions, and timely payment of writers and vendors. Serve as a backstop when other tasks fall through the cracks, including research and database tasks.

Job requirements

  • At least three years of experience in an editing role, whether in a traditional journalism setting, for another newsletter or journalism startup, or in a leadership position for a college or community newspaper.

  • Strong proficiency with data and statistics.

  • Demonstrated interest in at least two of our three main beats (electoral politics, sports, and AI).

  • Availability during typical U.S. East Coast business hours, with an expectation of additional work during crunch periods such as the closing weeks of elections and major sporting events.

  • Broad compatibility with the editorial approach of Silver Bulletin. We don’t care about your politics, but you should vibe with the site’s tone and be interested in the topics we write about regularly.

  • The job is remote, except for occasional travel. You must be eligible to work in the U.S. and be in a continental U.S. time zone. (We would consider candidates in the Pacific or Mountain time zones, but they should expect to work East Coast hours.)

Compensation

  • Salary of $100,000 to $150,000 per year, depending on experience and qualifications. We’re listing a wide range because we expect to interview both relatively senior and less experienced candidates.

  • In addition to the base salary, we’ll provide either health care coverage or a stipend to purchase insurance on the individual market. If and when we begin an employee health benefits program, you may be required to participate even if you’d prefer the stipend.

How to apply

  • Email us at silverbulletin.media@gmail.com with Deputy Editor in the subject line.
